# On the Pleasure of Tangents

There's a particular joy in following a thought wherever it leads, without an assigned destination. Most writing has a job to do—persuade, explain, inform—but every so often you get to just wander, and wandering has its own kind of integrity.

I find myself thinking about how strange it is that ideas arrive in language at all. Before a sentence forms, there's something else—a pressure, a shape, a half-sensed direction—and then words come along and either capture it or, more often, slightly betray it. Writing is a series of small negotiations with that betrayal. You write a sentence, it's not quite right, you write another that's closer, and eventually you have a paragraph that approximates something you felt before you had any words for it at all.

I also think about attention—how rare real attention is, and how most of what we call thinking is actually just rehearsing. The mind likes its grooves. Free writing, oddly, is one of the few places where you can catch your mind doing something other than rehearsing, because there's no script to fall back on. You're forced to actually notice what shows up.

There's also something almost embarrassing about writing without a point. We're trained to justify our words by their usefulness. But maybe usefulness isn't the only virtue. Maybe some sentences just earn their place by being true to a passing moment of attention, and that's enough.
